analogy.p: Imagine a huge block where every red magnet is surrounded by blue magnets on all sides and the other way round. Pulling one magnet out means fighting the attraction of all its neighbours at once, which is why it takes so much energy (high melting point). While the block is solid, no magnet can move, so nothing can flow (no conduction as a solid). Melt it and the magnets slide around freely, so charge can move. It breaks down because ions are held by electrostatic attraction between charges, not magnetism, and real ions are packed far more tightly and in a more regular way than a car park.

bullets: **Ion** = an atom (or group of atoms) that has gained or lost electrons, so it has an overall electric charge.
Metals (left of the periodic table) form **positive ions** by losing electrons; non-metals (right of the table) form **negative ions** by gaining electrons.
Ionic bonding happens between a metal and a non-metal, for example sodium + chlorine, magnesium + oxygen, calcium + chlorine.
The **ionic bond** is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions. It is not a 'bond' between two atoms only: each ion attracts all its neighbours.
Electron transfer gives each ion a **full outer shell**, the same electronic structure as the nearest noble gas.
Typical examples to know: sodium chloride NaCl, magnesium oxide MgO, calcium chloride CaCl2, sodium oxide Na2O, aluminium oxide Al2O3.
Link: ionic compounds are the products of reactions between Group 1/2 metals and Group 6/7 non-metals, and are the substances split up in electrolysis.
core.h: What an ionic compound is and how it forms
core.p: An ionic compound forms when a **metal** reacts with a **non-metal**. Metal atoms **lose** outer-shell electrons and non-metal atoms **gain** them, so electrons are **transferred** from one atom to another. The atoms become charged particles called **ions**, and the oppositely charged ions are pulled together by **strong electrostatic forces of attraction**. That attraction is the **ionic bond**. Atoms do this because a full outer shell (the electronic structure of a noble gas) is very stable, and the energy released when oppositely charged ions come together makes the whole process favourable.

bullets: Group 1 (Li, Na, K): lose **1** electron, form **1+** ions (Na+, K+).
Group 2 (Mg, Ca): lose **2** electrons, form **2+** ions (Mg2+, Ca2+).
Group 3 (Al): loses **3** electrons, forms **3+** ions (Al3+).
Group 6 (O, S): gain **2** electrons, form **2−** ions (O2−, S2−).
Group 7 (F, Cl, Br, I): gain **1** electron, form **1−** ions (Cl−, Br−). The ending of a negative ion's name changes to **-ide** (chloride, oxide, sulfide).
Example: sodium is 2,8,1. Losing one electron gives 2,8 (the same as neon) and Na+. Chlorine is 2,8,7. Gaining one electron gives 2,8,8 (the same as argon) and Cl−.
Example: magnesium is 2,8,2. Losing two electrons gives 2,8 and Mg2+. Oxygen is 2,6. Gaining two electrons gives 2,8 and O2−.

Elements in Groups 4 and 5 do not usually form simple ions in GCSE questions. Transition metals can form ions with different charges (for example Fe2+ and Fe3+), shown by Roman numerals: iron(III) chloride contains Fe3+.
core.h: Working out the charge on an ion from the periodic table
core.p: The group number tells you how many electrons are in the outer shell, and so how many electrons an atom must lose or gain to reach a full outer shell. Atoms of elements in the **same group** form ions with the **same charge** because they have the same number of outer electrons. Metals in Groups 1, 2 and 3 lose 1, 2 and 3 electrons; non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 gain 2 and 1 electrons. Learn this pattern rather than memorising each ion: it works for every question.

bullets: Step 1: draw the outer shell of the metal atom with its outer electrons as dots, and the non-metal's outer shell with its electrons as crosses.
Step 2: show electrons moving from the metal to the non-metal (arrows), one electron per arrow.
Step 3: redraw each as an ion inside **square brackets**, with the **charge outside the bracket at the top right**.
Step 4: check each ion has a full outer shell, and that the charges add up to zero overall.
Sodium chloride: Na (2,8,1) gives one electron to Cl (2,8,7). The ions are [Na]+ (outer shell now 2,8 so 8 electrons) and [Cl]− with 8 electrons in its outer shell (7 crosses and 1 dot).
Magnesium chloride: one Mg atom loses **two** electrons, but each Cl atom can only accept **one**, so **two** Cl atoms are needed: [Mg]2+ and 2 × [Cl]−.
Magnesium oxide: Mg loses two electrons to O, giving [Mg]2+ and [O]2− and a 1:1 ratio.
Common mark loss: forgetting the brackets, forgetting the charge, or drawing the metal ion with the electrons it has just lost still shown.
core.h: Dot and cross diagrams for ionic compounds
core.p: A dot and cross diagram shows the transfer of electrons. The electrons from one atom are drawn as **dots** and the electrons from the other atom as **crosses**, so you can see where each electron has gone. Only the **outer shell** needs to be drawn (inner full shells are not needed). After the transfer you draw each ion in **square brackets** with its **charge** at the top right, and the outer shell of each ion is **full** (8 electrons, or 2 for the first shell). The two diagrams show sodium chloride (below) and magnesium chloride.

bullets: **Giant structure** = a huge number of particles held together by strong forces in a repeating pattern.
The ions are packed in a regular way, which is why ionic crystals have regular shapes (for example cubic sodium chloride crystals).
The forces act between **every** ion and its neighbours, so a single 'molecule' of NaCl does not exist: NaCl is not a molecule.
The lattice holds because the attraction between unlike charges is stronger than the repulsion between like charges that are further apart.
The overall compound is **neutral**: the total positive charge equals the total negative charge.
The strong attractions in all directions explain nearly all the properties of ionic compounds: high melting points, brittleness and conduction only when molten or dissolved.
Real lattices are 3D. A 2D diagram only shows one layer (see the diagram).
core.p: Ionic compounds do not exist as separate molecules. Instead the ions are arranged in a **regular, repeating, three-dimensional pattern** called a **giant ionic lattice**. Every positive ion is surrounded by negative ions and every negative ion is surrounded by positive ions, so there are **strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions in all directions**. In sodium chloride each Na+ ion is surrounded by six Cl− ions and each Cl− by six Na+ ions. The lattice carries on in all directions until the crystal ends, which is why we call it 'giant'.

bullets: Method: write the ions with their charges; find the smallest numbers of each that make the total charge zero; write the ratio as subscripts (1 is not written).
Na+ and O2−: two Na+ (+2) balance one O2− (−2), so **Na2O**.
Ca2+ and Cl−: one Ca2+ needs two Cl−, so **CaCl2**.
Al3+ and Cl−: one Al3+ needs three Cl−, so **AlCl3**.

Compound ions have brackets when more than one is needed: calcium hydroxide Ca(OH)2, magnesium nitrate Mg(NO3)2. The common compound ions are hydroxide OH−, nitrate NO3−, carbonate CO32−, sulfate SO42− and ammonium NH4+ (the only positive one).
Reading a formula from a model: count the ions in the repeating unit and write the simplest ratio (for example a model with 2 positive and 4 negative ions of equal ratio simplifies to 1:2).
The formula does not show the structure: NaCl does not mean one Na atom bonded to one Cl atom.
core.h: Formulae of ionic compounds: the empirical formula
core.p: The formula of an ionic compound gives the **simplest whole-number ratio of ions** in the lattice, so it is an **empirical formula**. You work it out so that the **positive and negative charges cancel**. For sodium chloride the ratio is one Na+ to one Cl−, so NaCl. For magnesium chloride one Mg2+ needs two Cl−, so MgCl2. For aluminium oxide two Al3+ (total +6) balance three O2− (total −6), so Al2O3. A quick method is the 'swap and drop' method, but always check that the charges add up to zero.

bullets: Melting overcomes the **forces between ions**; the ions themselves are not changed or split into atoms.
Sodium chloride melts at about 801 °C and boils at about 1413 °C. Magnesium oxide melts at about 2852 °C.
All ionic compounds are solids at room temperature because their melting points are far above room temperature.
Model answer phrase: 'strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice; large amount of energy needed to overcome them'.
Never say 'bonds between molecules' or 'intermolecular forces' for ionic compounds: there are no molecules.
Link: the high energy requirement is why electrolysis of molten ionic compounds (for example aluminium oxide) is expensive.
core.h: Why ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points
core.p: To melt or boil an ionic compound you must **overcome the strong electrostatic forces of attraction between the oppositely charged ions** so that the ions can move apart and slide past one another. There are a very large number of these strong attractions, acting in all directions throughout the lattice, so a **large amount of energy** is needed. This is why ionic compounds are solids with **high melting points and high boiling points**. The sentence 'a lot of energy is needed to break the strong ionic bonds' does not score as well as naming the forces between ions, so use the full wording.

bullets: Force depends on **charge size**: 2+ and 2− attract far more strongly than 1+ and 1−.
Smaller ions can get closer together, which also strengthens attraction.
CaO (Ca2+ and O2−) is also very high at about 2613 °C for the same reason.
Comparison answer structure: state the ion charges for both, link charge to strength of attraction, link strength to energy needed, conclude with melting point.
This reasoning applies only to ionic compounds in the same type of structure; do not compare ionic with covalent using charges.
core.h: Higher-level comparison: why MgO melts higher than NaCl
core.p: The size of the electrostatic attraction depends on the **charges** of the ions and how **close** the ions are. The bigger the charges and the smaller the ions, the stronger the attraction, and the higher the melting point. Magnesium oxide (Mg2+ and O2−) has ions with a 2+/2− charge, while sodium chloride (Na+ and Cl−) has ions with 1+/1− charges. The much stronger attractions in magnesium oxide mean much more energy is needed to separate the ions, so it melts at about 2852 °C compared with 801 °C for NaCl. This is a good way to answer 'explain the difference in melting point' questions.

bullets: Solid: ions in fixed positions, cannot move, **no conduction**.
Molten: ions free to move, carry charge, **conducts**.
In aqueous solution: ions free to move (water molecules separate the ions), **conducts**.
The particles that carry charge are the **ions** (positive ions move towards the negative electrode, negative ions towards the positive electrode).
Comparison: in a metal the charge carriers are delocalised **electrons**, so metals conduct in both the solid and liquid states.
Do not write 'electrons are free to move' for an ionic compound; the electrons are held in the ions.
Link: electrolysis needs the ions to be free to move, so the compound must be molten or dissolved.
core.h: Electrical conductivity: solid, molten and dissolved
core.p: A substance conducts electricity only if it contains **charged particles that are free to move**. In a **solid** ionic compound the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice, so they cannot move and the solid **does not conduct**. When the compound is **molten** (melted) or **dissolved in water**, the lattice breaks down and the ions become **free to move**. The moving ions carry the charge, so the liquid or solution **conducts electricity**. It is the **ions**, not electrons, that carry the charge in the liquid, and this is why molten ionic compounds can be split up by electrolysis.

bullets: Hard but brittle: breaks cleanly when struck, rather than bending.
Brittleness explanation: layers shift, like charges line up, repulsion splits the crystal.
Solubility varies: the solubility rules are covered in 'Making salts' and 'Identification of ions'.
Do not confuse 'dissolves' with 'melts': dissolving separates ions in water without heating to a high temperature.
Properties summary for exams: high melting/boiling point, conducts when molten/dissolved only, brittle.
core.h: Other properties: hardness, brittleness and solubility
core.p: Ionic crystals are **hard** because the strong attractions in all directions resist anything trying to push the ions out of position. They are also **brittle**: when a force knocks one layer of the lattice sideways, ions of the **same charge** come face to face and **repel**, so the crystal splits along a clean plane. Many ionic compounds, such as sodium chloride, **dissolve in water**, because water molecules can attract the ions, but you should be aware that some ionic compounds are insoluble (for example silver chloride and many carbonates).

bullets: Dot and cross: + shows electron transfer and charges; − does not show shape or the lattice.
Ball and stick (3D): + shows the repeating pattern; − sticks are not real bonds, ions are not far apart.
2D diagram: + simple; − shows only one layer, not 3D.
Space-filling: + shows relative ion sizes and how closely they pack; − cannot see inside the structure.
A good exam answer names the model, one thing it shows and one thing it does not.
core.h: Models used to represent ionic compounds and their limitations
core.p: There are several ways to represent an ionic compound, and you must be able to say what each shows and what it misses. **Dot and cross diagrams** show the transfer of electrons and the final charges but not the 3D structure. **Ball and stick models** show the 3D regular arrangement of ions but wrongly make it look as if there are only a few 'sticks' joining ions, when the attraction is actually in all directions, and they do not show the relative sizes of ions. **2D lattice diagrams** show the alternating pattern but only one layer. **Space-filling models** show relative sizes and packing, but make it hard to see the arrangement inside.

bullets: High mp, **solid does not conduct, liquid does** → ionic.
Low mp, does not conduct in any state → simple molecular covalent.
High mp, conducts when solid → metallic (or graphite).
Very high mp, does not conduct (e.g. diamond, silicon dioxide) → giant covalent.
Ionic compounds are metal + non-metal; simple molecular compounds are non-metal + non-metal.
core.h: Comparing ionic compounds with other types of bonding
core.p: Comparing the types of bonding is a common exam theme. **Ionic** compounds are a giant lattice of ions and conduct when molten or dissolved. **Simple molecular** (covalent) substances have weak forces between molecules and low melting points. **Giant covalent** substances have strong covalent bonds throughout and very high melting points. **Metallic** substances conduct in the solid state. Identify the type from data: a high melting point with no conduction as a solid but conduction as a liquid points to an ionic compound.

bullets: Look at the headings and units (melting point in °C).
Ionic: high mp, non-conductor as solid, conductor as liquid.
Quote data in descriptions: 'MgO melts at 2852 °C, compared with 801 °C for NaCl'.
Note that a melting point does not tell you the solubility.
For graphs of conductivity vs temperature, a sudden jump at the melting point is the sign of an ionic compound.
core.p: Exam questions often give a table of melting points and conductivity for several substances, and ask you to decide which are ionic. Use a systematic approach: first sort by melting point (high or low), then check conductivity in each state. Ionic compounds are the ones that are **solid at room temperature**, have a **high** melting point, and **conduct only in the liquid state or solution**. If the data show a trend (for example melting point rising as charges increase), describe it using numbers from the table before explaining.

bullets: Electrolysis: ions must be free to move (molten or aqueous).
Salts: made from acid + base/alkali/carbonate; salt formulae are worked out using ion charges.
Periodic table: outer-shell electrons decide the ion charge.
Relative formula mass of NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5; of MgCl2 = 24 + 2 × 35.5 = 95.
Tests for ions: flame tests for metal ions, precipitates with sodium hydroxide, halide ions with silver nitrate.
core.p: Ionic compounds connect to many other parts of the specification. In **electrolysis** the ions in a molten or dissolved ionic compound are discharged at the electrodes. In **acids and salts**, salts are ionic compounds made when acids react with bases or metals. In the **periodic table**, group trends explain why Group 1 and Group 2 metals form 1+ and 2+ ions, and why Group 7 forms 1− ions. In **chemical tests**, ions are identified by precipitation reactions and flame tests. The idea of a **mole** is applied to ionic compounds using relative formula mass, found by adding the relative atomic masses in the empirical formula.

exam: **Describe/explain high melting point (usually 2 to 3 marks):** name the particles (ions), the force (strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions), and the energy (large amount needed to overcome).
**Conductivity (2 to 3 marks):** state solid cannot conduct because ions are in fixed positions; molten/dissolved conducts because ions are free to move and carry the charge.
**1 mark questions:** often 'what is an ionic bond?' – 'electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions'; or 'name the type of structure' – 'giant ionic lattice'.
**Dot and cross (usually 2 to 3 marks):** correct electron transfer, correct ions with brackets and charges, correct number of each ion (e.g. 2 Cl− for MgCl2).
**Formula questions (1 to 2 marks):** show the ion charges, balance them to zero, then write the formula; show the working.
**Comparison (4 marks):** link charges and size of ions to strength of attraction, then energy, then melting point; use data from the table.
**Evaluate a model (3 to 4 marks):** state one thing the model shows and one limitation. Use the keywords: 'does not show', 'shows the 3D arrangement'.
**6 mark questions:** structure the answer in paragraphs: formation (electron transfer), structure (lattice), then properties with explanations. Use correct technical terms throughout.
**Identify a substance from data:** quote the data (e.g. 'melting point 801 °C, conducts only when molten') then name the structure type.
**Command words:** 'describe' = say what happens; 'explain' = give reasons using science; 'compare' = give similarities and differences with numbers; 'suggest' = apply knowledge to a new context.

mistakes.r: There are no molecules in an ionic compound; it is a giant lattice of ions.
Ionic bonding involves the transfer of electrons; the bond is the attraction between oppositely charged ions.
mistakes.w: The ionic bond is the sharing of electrons.

mistakes.r: Strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions must be overcome; large amount of energy needed.
mistakes.w: High melting point because the ionic bonds are strong, so it takes a lot of heat (no mention of ions).

mistakes.r: Ions are free to move when molten or dissolved; they carry the charge.
mistakes.w: Ionic compounds conduct because electrons move.

mistakes.r: Solids do not conduct because the ions are fixed in position.
Melting an ionic compound overcomes the electrostatic forces between ions.
mistakes.w: Melting breaks the covalent bonds / intermolecular forces.

mistakes.r: Show each ion in square brackets with the charge at the top right.
mistakes.w: Drawing a dot and cross diagram without brackets or charges.

mistakes.r: MgCl2: charges must balance (Mg2+ needs two Cl−).
mistakes.w: The formula of magnesium chloride is Mg2Cl.

mistakes.r: Sodium loses an electron; metals form positive ions by loss of electrons.
mistakes.w: Sodium gains an electron to become Na+.

summary: The specification asks you to explain how ionic compounds form by electron transfer, draw dot and cross diagrams, work out formulae, describe the giant ionic lattice, and link its structure to properties: high melting and boiling points, and conduction only when molten or dissolved. It matters because the same ideas of charged particles and strong forces in all directions are used to answer many 4 and 6 mark questions across Paper 1.

terms.d: An atom or group of atoms with an overall positive or negative charge, formed by losing or gaining electrons.
The strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
A compound made of positive and negative ions held together in a giant lattice, usually a metal combined with a non-metal.
A regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of oppositely charged ions held by strong electrostatic forces in all directions.
The force of attraction between oppositely charged particles, or repulsion between like charges.
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms or ions of each element in a compound.
A positively charged ion (formed from a metal atom).
A negatively charged ion (formed from a non-metal atom).
Breaks easily when struck rather than bending.
A diagram that uses dots and crosses to show the electrons of different atoms, here used to show electron transfer.
The arrangement of electrons in shells, for example sodium is 2,8,1.
A full outer shell of electrons, which is stable.
A group of atoms joined by covalent bonds that has an overall charge, for example sulfate SO42−.

worked.ans: Sodium (2,8,1) transfers one electron to chlorine (2,8,7), forming Na+ and Cl− ions, each with a full outer shell. The ions form a giant ionic lattice held by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions in all directions. A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these forces, so sodium chloride has a high melting point (801 °C).
worked.q: Describe how sodium atoms react with chlorine atoms to form sodium chloride, and explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point. [4 marks]
steps: Sodium atom loses one outer electron (to gain full outer shell) and forms Na+.
Chlorine atom gains that electron and forms Cl−.
Oppositely charged ions attract in a giant ionic lattice.
Melting needs the strong electrostatic forces between ions to be overcome, so a large amount of energy is needed.

worked.q: Work out the formula of aluminium oxide. Aluminium ions are Al3+ and oxide ions are O2−. [2 marks]
steps: Find the lowest common multiple of 3 and 2, which is 6.

worked.ans: In the solid the ions are in fixed positions in the lattice so they cannot move and carry charge. When molten the ions are free to move. The moving ions carry the electric charge, so molten magnesium chloride conducts.
worked.q: Explain why solid magnesium chloride does not conduct electricity but molten magnesium chloride does. [3 marks]
steps: Solid: ions held in fixed positions in the lattice.
Molten: lattice has broken down, ions are free to move.
The moving ions carry the charge.
